title: AI and Assets Question
author: Desperate_Crew9840
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’d like to ask for your honest opinions **- no AI talk, no self-promotion, just a genuine question that’s been on my mind.**

I’m both a content creator and a content consumer. For the past few years, I’ve been uploading various game assets to platforms like itch and GDM. However, lately I feel like AI has significantly changed the landscape and completely disrupted the market.

A lot of spaces now feel flooded and diluted with what many would call "AI slop." Because of this, even high-quality work can sometimes get dismissed simply because it’s associated with AI in general - even when it actually involves real effort and careful production. At the same time, traditional handcrafted work doesn’t necessarily seem to be gaining more value either, at least from what I can observe.

I don’t feel like I have a clear picture of the current market anymore - the conditions and "rules of the game" have changed quite a lot compared to a few years ago with the AI boom. That’s why I’d really appreciate your input, whether that’s advice, experience, insights, stories, or anything relevant.

Thank you in advance to anyone who takes the time to engage with this post - even a few thoughtful responses would really help me understand the direction things are heading.

So my main questions are:

**Where do you think it’s currently worth uploading content (2D, 3D, audio, graphics, etc.) where there is still real demand and some form of proportional return on effort? What platforms or directions would you personally recommend as the most viable today?**

**Conversely, where do you usually download or source assets from? What platforms are currently "mainstream" among developers - places that are not just unfiltered AI dumps, but have some level of structure, quality control, and usability? Even if AI content exists there, the platform still feels organized and practical to use.**

In one sentence: what are your favorite platforms (for both uploading and downloading developer-related assets or content) where there is active traffic, real community, and genuinely useful content?

I really appreciate any guidance or perspectives.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body: OK, thanks! Who are your favorite creators, what kind of content do you usually look for, and who are you specifically very satisfied with and would strongly recommend?

replies.author: DamnageBeats
replies.body: Ansimuz for side scroller, final boss blues for top-down, winlu is good. Just search game assets on itch.io.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body: Thank you! I’ve spent quite a few years on the platform both as a creator and a user, and right now I’m specifically interested in who others prefer and recommend.

comments.author: Just-Investigator-20
comments.body: I hold a slightly different perspective: given that various platforms are already inundated with massive amounts of AI-generated junk, this trend is, in reality, unlikely to be reversed—it will only intensify. Rather than searching for a "sanctuary" free from this noise, it would be more productive to explore how you can leverage AI to amplify the impact of your existing skills—perhaps by creating content that is more polished than ever before, or by producing resource packages of greater scope and volume. In short, the goal should be to find ways to create content that you previously considered beyond your capabilities—work that those with no prior experience could not possibly produce using AI alone. I believe this is the most effective strategy for competing in the age of AI.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body: Interesting advice. By the time OP gets good enough to start doing things beyond his previous capabilities, AI would probably catch up and get even better than him.

replies.author: Just-Investigator-20
replies.body: To be honest, this is precisely what makes me feel a sense of sadness right now. I first encountered an Apple II-compatible computer back in the fourth grade and became instantly captivated by programming—a passion that has now spanned over forty years. Yet, it was only this year that I realized the practical utility of the coding skills I had accumulated over all that time has dwindled to nearly zero. I doubt I’ve written a single line of code by hand all year, and it seems unlikely that there will be many opportunities to do so in the future, either. But what is one to do? Should I go out and find a project that strictly forbids the use of AI—one that demands manual coding—simply to keep my skills alive? Or should I embrace AI as quickly as possible and embark on a new phase? I chose the latter path, and—remarkably—my productivity over these past few months has actually surpassed that of the previous several years combined. Many things I previously wouldn't have dared to imagine or attempt are now within reach. If AI truly performs better than I do on my own, how can I possibly expect to avoid being replaced? Nevertheless, I am confident that my forty years of development experience will enable me to stay ahead of the curve compared to most people when it comes to leveraging AI. A new beginning at age 53.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
I'm in a similar boat, although I'm a little bit younger. The way I see it, we either keep evolving with the world, or we perish. There's no point in trying to latch on the past. I still miss the old DOS days and part of me wishes computers wouldn't have improved much beyond that.

Tbh just adjust, go with the times and if you really have the itch to code manually, do a side project. For me personally, I prefer building faster over manually writing code, so I'll take the AI.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
I’d also like to join in on this discussion as well. Since I was the one who originally asked the question, and you all took the time and effort to respond to it, I feel like I should also put effort into the conversation. And honestly, I genuinely enjoy talking about these things, because to this day I still live mentally in the computer and gaming world of the 1990s and early 2000s.

I even keep one or two separate PCs around running Windows XP and Windows 7 just so those old games and applications can still run properly, and so that entire era can remain part of my everyday life. After all, a lot of older software simply doesn’t run anymore on Windows 10 or 11.

But over time I realized that alongside the nostalgia and all the beautiful memories, we still have to keep moving forward. Everything from the past that we now deeply love was once “the future” too - something people had to open themselves up to at the time. And this new future is here now as well, and we need to be open to it too.

AI helps tremendously with everyday tasks, projects, and countless other things. Not to mention that it’s an endless source of humor. Whether it’s text, images, video, or music, it constantly gives us reasons to laugh until we cry.

But even with all that, nothing can truly replace childhood memories and everything that computers and technology gave us during those years. Maybe that’s part of the beauty of it all - that with today’s technology and AI, we can revisit many things from the past and elevate them to a whole new level :)

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
First of all, sincere congratulations on starting over at the age of 53. I genuinely enjoyed reading your comment, especially since I myself have been a serious and enthusiastic computer user for more than 30 years, and programming has been part of my life for around 25 years now. I still have plenty of books packed away in boxes from the days of Turbo Pascal, BASIC, and procedural programming.

You raised some very important questions. If I wanted to take a humorous approach to it: everyone is worried about whether AI will take our jobs? Honestly, it can take the work - just don’t let it take the money that comes from it :)

But speaking seriously, I do think this is roughly the direction things are heading: integrating AI into everyday life in a way that it works for us and instead of us, while the rewards and results still remain ours.

I don’t think maintaining individual knowledge is pointless at all. Cars already have self driving features, yet most cars are still driven by people, and autonomous driving is ultimately just a feature that still requires human supervision and decision making. I think programming is heading in a similar direction.

People are already building large and serious systems with tools like Codex and other AI solutions, while at the same time the review and supervision of AI generated work and output is becoming an increasingly important industry or segment in itself. I keep seeing more and more of this across the internet.

I personally don’t think the human factor will ever become completely removable or unnecessary. We just need to be on the right side of this entire process - or revolution.

I’m personally trying to do exactly that as well, and that’s also why I’m here taking part in conversations like this one.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
I’m trying to interpret your comment as completely positive guidance, and respond to it from that perspective. Every day I try to work on things that represent growth compared to my previous abilities, and the game asset market is only one small slice of that activity when looking at the bigger picture.

We’ve been using AI on a daily basis since the very beginning, ever since it entered mainstream awareness, and we’ve been trying to keep up with it on every level. I also have no problem opening up to new things - if necessary, I can let go of attachment to older directions and adapt, evolve, and move forward. That’s exactly why I’m here and why I asked these questions in the first place.

I don’t underestimate the capabilities of AI, but I also think it’s important not to overestimate them either. We’re not living in The Matrix yet, and Skynet hasn’t become self aware - AI still needs to be kept under fairly strong control and supervision. You still have to “hold its hand” in order to get meaningful, usable output and content from it.

What I simply want to see realistically is where the line is between people deciding to create content themselves through prompting, and where they instead choose to buy pre made content from someone else or download it from somewhere. And based on individual experiences, I’m also interested in how this whole phenomenon is affecting the market and personal perspectives.

I still feel that it has seriously influenced the market, and not only because something is handmade or AI generated, but because the entire supply - demand balance has shifted and become disrupted. The focus has changed, everyday habits have changed, and so have people’s routines. The same game asset packs that could easily generate a few thousand dollars a few years ago still bring in something useful today, but the demand for them is noticeably lower.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
I'm replying to the commenter who said that you need to create that has been too hard to create until now. If it has been too hard, that means that not many humans got the skills to do it, it was too time consuming, or both. That comment assumes that you will somehow be able to pull out a masterpiece out of your behind. It is extremely naive and unrealistic.

Regarding AI capabilities. Look at how bad ChatGPT 3 was when it was released and compare it to what models are able to do today. Then count the number of years that has elapsed since it was published. 

Now go and figure out how many years it will take you to get the skills previous commenter alluded to, plus how much time it would take you to create such assets. Interpolate how fast AI has been evolving to where it's going to be in such time. That will help you figure out whether you're still going to have a market by then.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
I understand the situation, and I’m glad this topic has sparked discussion and brought different viewpoints to the surface.  
I reply to every comment after having originally asked the question, because I believe that is the fair approach, and I genuinely value all perspectives. You also directly addressed me in your comment, which makes me feel even more personally involved in the discussion.  
  
That said, from a professional standpoint, I find your previous comment, as well as this one, to be somewhat overly pessimistic and deterministic, which in my view results in a rather one-sided interpretation of the situation. There is truth in what you are saying-the pace of AI development is undeniably fast, and I acknowledge and agree with that-but it is also important not to overlook the fact that markets and demand are changing alongside this evolution.

It is important to recognize that the argument suggesting “by the time you become skilled enough, AI will already be better than you” assumes a static world where competition happens along a single dimension: raw capability versus raw capability. In reality, markets do not function in this way. What matters is not simply who can produce something “better” in a purely technical sense, but how well that output fits into a specific use case, how reliable and consistent it is, how easily it can be integrated, and how much real value it creates within a given workflow or product.

AI development is not a uniform process that simply “overrides everything.” Instead, it creates new bottlenecks: while it drastically reduces certain production costs, it simultaneously increases the importance of other areas such as decision-making, direction, quality control, and system integration-areas where human involvement remains highly significant. Because of this, the competition is not simply a matter of humans versus AI, but rather about who can build effective systems that combine these elements in a meaningful way.

Although this discussion has moved somewhat away from my original question, I still appreciate your response and the time you took to share your perspective, and I hope you also find value in my attempt to present a more objective viewpoint.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
What makes your viewpoint more objective, exactly? That claim is a little bit arrogant, isn't it? I understand that what I said is not what you wanted to hear, but here's a tip: if you don't want people to tell you what you don't want to hear, don't ask questions in a public forum. Find an echo chamber instead.

Also, did you write this with AI?

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
**Please** try to keep the discussion on a professional level instead of making it personal or projecting your emotions/frustrations onto others. Your comment comes across as fairly aggressive in tone, but I’m not interested in going down that road. If I wanted pointless arguments, I would go into some random Facebook group - I came here hoping for constructive discussion and exchange of perspectives.

Just like in my previous replies, I would also like to maintain a certain level of normality and objectivity here. Please read my previous comment again carefully. I did not say that my opinion is completely objective - I said that I strive toward objectivity. I try to do that by thinking, researching, and weighing different perspectives before writing and posting my comments. *(Which is something I can also recommend to others.)*

I wrote the text myself, using my own thoughts, exactly as I am doing now. However, for research, evaluation, and analytical purposes, I do sometimes use AI tools. I did so in this case as well regarding the entire Reddit discussion, by comparing the opinions of 3 separate AI systems using the following question *(worth trying by the way, just a tip!)*:  
“Analyze, based on the commenters’ opinions, who is more correct and who is being more realistic.”

**Unfortunately**, your replies consistently scored around 4.5/10 or at most 5/10 compared to several other participants who landed around the 8-9 range. See? That is objectivity. On a public forum, I can also receive dismissive *(or arrogant!?)* responses to well-structured questions.

What is subjective, however, is that due to your communication style, I’m no longer interested in engaging with your replies going forward. Since Reddit is a public platform, of course you are free to continue posting them if you wish, but I wanted you to know that I’ll simply ignore them from now on because I personally find them unhelpful and unnecessary - both from an objective and subjective perspective.

I prefer to spend my energy on useful things and useful people. See? That’s how AI should actually be used: to help point us in the right direction. The control remains on the human side, while the machine handles the “dirty work“ for us 😉

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
I'm not emotional, nor am I frustrated. I have just openly pointed out your fallacies and delusions. It's not my fault that you can't take objective criticism.

Go be delusional with your AI slop somewhere else, please.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
You wrote some interesting points, and I basically agree that we should use AI as a tool to elevate things to a higher level. I know this is a divisive topic, and I’m not anti-AI. In fact, I’m disappointed to see that the high-quality work we create - where AI plays an important role - gets lumped together with the kind of 1-2 prompt AI trash that people instantly spam onto the internet without any filtering or review.

I’m also someone who, together with the people I work with on projects, built an extremely powerful setup, and we’re currently working on automation workflows, so I absolutely see the amazing potential in all of this. At the same time, I can’t ignore the fact that interest in my older game asset packs on itch has completely changed. Recently I’ve tried everything to refresh and improve them, and those earlier assets barely contain any AI at all - they were all handmade.

I’m always thinking about which direction would be the most worthwhile to move toward - something that has real potential. From what I see, the classic “uploading game asset packs” approach doesn’t necessarily seem like a particularly profitable or ambitious path anymore. Where do you see the biggest opportunities?

Thank you for your reply and for sharing your opinion in detail!

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body:
I was looking recently for art into a card game, but it was really hard to find things that I could adapt for my game, even if I was willing to spend some money. I found one guy who made art in the volume I wanted, it was $60 dollars for batches of 100 card images (I didnt need the animations, but I needed good illustrations), and on each batch I would use probably 1/3 being optimistic. Anyway, that was on the unity store, I still check that from time to time.
I also check itch.io for cheaper stuff, but it is kind of hard to navigate their interface.
But most of my money went for humble bundle and the cheap stuff I can get in bulk, even tough I never use those - most of what I've bought was 3D environment assets, and I see now that I'll never get to use those.
Thats my take as a potential client. For the card engine I do have a solution bought from a bundle a while ago, but I decided to produce one for my own using gemini - I dont think I would risk a code asset unless it was a big solution, like Odin was (last time I've spent money on the asset store).
I'm a hobbyist programmer that dont finish projects and buy assets mainly on how cheap they are and how much they can benefit me, thats part of the demographic that pays for stuff, but not the main costumer I believe.

replies.author: Desperate_Crew9840
replies.body:
Thank you for your reply, and for explaining things from a professional perspective while also sharing your personal habits and story. What you wrote was genuinely interesting to read.

I’ve also been thinking for a long time about creating some kind of card game, but I never quite get to the point of actually making it. Back in the day we were huge fans during the Yu-Gi-Oh! era. We played it both in real life and on PC all the time. And beyond that, in the 1990s we also spent countless hours playing Magic: The Gathering. If there’s one area where AI feels absolutely perfect, it’s probably creating illustrations for these kinds of cards.  
  
And then there were games like Etherlords and similar titles as well. A lot of things inspired me over the years, but I still haven’t fully reached the point where I actually make my own project. Even so, it still crosses my mind almost every week, and I haven’t given up on the idea yet.

What you mentioned about commissioning someone to create something custom is also interesting, because that’s something I personally haven’t really done before. Usually I would imagine an idea, create it myself, upload it, and then observe what people seemed to want more of. At the same time, several people have already suggested to me that as a creator it’s worth moving more toward custom and individual requests. So in that sense your comment was genuinely inspiring to me as well, which I’d also like to thank you for.

And on another note: I also happen to have one or two paid card packs myself. I don’t know whether you’d actually have any use for them since they’re French suited playing cards, but simply because you took the time to reply to my question, I’d genuinely be happy to give you a copy for free if you’d like to share a contact method ;)

P.S.: One of my constant and eternal flaws has also always been that I rarely finished most of my projects either - even when entering serious competitions, I usually only barely managed to complete them at the very last moment. It’s difficult to maintain that initial motivation all the way through, but not impossible.
